what_it_does: Running large language models on very long documents or conversations (100,000 words or more) is brutally slow and memory-hungry because the model must look back at every prior word on every new generation step. LServe cuts both the computation and memory costs at the same time by teaching the model to selectively skip large chunks of its own memory — without retraining the model and without meaningfully hurting accuracy.
method_in_detail:
The problem. When a language model generates each new word, it runs an 'attention' operation — essentially asking: which earlier words matter right now? For very long inputs, this becomes the dominant bottleneck, consuming over 75% of runtime at 128,000-token contexts. LServe attacks this with two complementary forms of skipping, unified into a single framework.

Static sparsity — heads that never look far. The attention computation is split across dozens of parallel 'heads,' each looking at the history in a slightly different way. LServe identifies (once, offline, using a published technique called DuoAttention) that roughly half the heads only ever care about a few recent words and a small set of very early 'anchor' words. These streaming heads are given a fixed, cheap pattern — they always skip the vast middle of the history. Both types of heads are then handled in a single fused GPU program that skips the absent blocks entirely, achieving up to 1.7x real speedup over doing them separately.

Dynamic sparsity — picking which pages matter right now. For the remaining 'dense' heads that do need to look far back, LServe avoids loading all stored past key-value pairs (the model's running memory of prior words). Instead, the history is divided into fixed physical memory pages (large, for hardware efficiency) but scored using finer logical sub-pages (small, for accuracy). Each sub-page's importance is estimated cheaply by comparing the current query against precomputed per-page min/max key summaries — a dot-product trick. Only the top-ranked physical pages are loaded. Because consecutive generated words tend to attend to the same pages (temporal locality of natural language), the page-selection result is reused across several generation steps without recomputation, reducing selector overhead by 4x.

The catch. Larger physical pages are better for memory bandwidth but hurt page-selection accuracy; the hierarchical two-level scheme decouples these concerns, letting the hardware use big pages while scoring at fine granularity.

The result. Versus vLLM (the standard baseline), LServe speeds up the initial processing phase by up to 2.9x and the word-by-word generation phase by 1.3–2.1x, with no measurable accuracy loss on long-context benchmarks.
